extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, editorial teams, and journal managers who design peer review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and implementing a structured reviewer feedback form and process for academic journals to improve consistency, clarity, and usefulness of peer review reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness of the literature review
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the literature review is comprehensive, up-to-date, and appropriate for the manuscript topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a key criterion to consider covering in structured peer review questions. Example question: 'Is the literature review comprehensive, up-to-date, and appropriate for the manuscript topic?' Editors should decide whether to require a response. This maps to the manuscript's contextual grounding and demonstrates whether prior work has been adequately considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor and quality of statistical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate methodological rigor, appropriateness of study design, and quality/correctness of statistical analyses where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prompts such as whether methods are described in sufficient detail to allow another researcher to reproduce the work. Malički recommends focusing reviewers on methodological, analytical aspects and asking them to note methodological flaws. Ask reviewers to comment specifically if elements of the research methodology appear flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of interpretation and support for conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the authors' interpretation of the results is clear and if study conclusions are supported by the data and study design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly ask whether the interpretation of results and study conclusions are supported by the data and/or study design. Encourage reviewers to point to specific mismatches between claims and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the perceived replicability and/or reproducibility of the study based on methods and reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the methods are described sufficiently to allow another researcher to reproduce the work. This may overlap with methodological rigor, but should be framed to capture whether sufficient detail and transparency exist for replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to journal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the manuscript fits the journal's stated scope and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include as an explicit question so editors can quickly triage submissions. This helps maintain fit and reduces reviewer effort on out-of-scope manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance and contribution to the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the significance of the findings and the level of contribution the manuscript makes to its field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be asked as a high-level Likert or overall question (e.g., 'To what extent does this manuscript offer a significant contribution?'). Note Malički's suggestion that novelty/impact are sometimes handled by editors to reduce reviewer workload, but many journals still include this as a reviewer prompt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required overall assessment (quality rating and publication recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mandatory overall manuscript quality rating (e.g., 1–5) plus a required publication recommendation (Accept, Reject, or Revise & Resubmit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide recommends all journals ask these required overall assessment questions. A manuscript quality rating gives editors a quick snapshot of confidence; a required recommendation ensures clarity on the reviewer's view of next steps. Example formats: numeric rubric (1–5) and categorical recommendation (Accept/Reject/Revise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question formatting — Likert scale for high-level agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Likert-scale questions (usually 5- or 7-point) to gauge agreement with statements about high-level manuscript criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for assessing items requiring a degree of agreement (e.g., 'To what extent does this manuscript offer a significant contribution?'). Likert items produce comparable data and are quick for reviewers, but should be paired with targets for which items to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question formatting — open response prompts for constructive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide open-ended text boxes for reviewers to give detailed, constructive feedback on specific aspects of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open responses enable critical commentary (e.g., flagging flawed methodology). But the guide warns that too many open-ended questions can lead to short, low-quality answers; aim for fewer high-value open prompts rather than many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Require reviewers to indicate if they feel they lack the expertise to assess particular aspects of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask reviewers to declare whether they can sufficiently address each feedback form question and to note hesitations about their knowledge level. This helps editors know when additional input or a different reviewer is needed and encourages forthright assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of reviewer focus (methods/analysis/interpretation vs. novelty/formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define that reviewers should primarily focus on methodological, analytical, and interpretative aspects, while novelty, potential impact, language, and formatting may be handled by editors or automated tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide relays Malički's recommendation that shifting non-methodological tasks away from reviewers can reduce reviewer workload and improve focus. Editors should decide which domains to include for reviewers and which to handle separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted pyramid question structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize reviewer questions from the most fundamental assessment criteria down to 'nice-to-have' or optional items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with essential questions needed for the manuscript to move forward, then progress to secondary items (e.g., writing quality or style) that might be optional. This helps ensure critical judgments are captured even if reviewers provide limited responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize open-ended questions to reduce reviewer burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the number of required open-ended questions so reviewers can provide more thorough responses to fewer prompts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are busy; too many mandatory text boxes may yield brief, unhelpful comments. Aim to provide a framework for essential aspects in as few questions as possible to maximize depth over breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish review questions and (optionally) review reports for transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the review form questions public on the journal website, and consider publishing review reports alongside accepted articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing questions helps authors and reviewers know expectations in advance and increases transparency. Publishing reports allows readers to judge how a paper was assessed and enables research on peer-review practices, per Malički's suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect feedback and iterate (monitor & refine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan to assess outcomes of the structured peer review process and iteratively refine the feedback form based on stakeholder input and metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the reviewer form as a living document. Collect feedback from reviewers, authors, and editors during pilots; run periodic check-in surveys; and use data to adjust criteria, questions, or reviewer training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor peer review performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Track quantitative and qualitative indicators such as reviewer experience, author satisfaction, and editorial decision times to evaluate the structured process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key areas to monitor include: Are reviewers finding the template easy to use? Are authors satisfied with feedback quality? Is decision time improving? Use these data points and the EASE recommendations to guide improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sample essential questions for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer concrete example questions to guide reviewers on what to address (e.g., objectives clarity, literature comprehensiveness, interpretation support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example questions from the article: 'Have the authors clearly articulated the primary purpose/objective(s)?' 'Is the literature review comprehensive, up-to-date, and appropriate?' 'Are the interpretation of results and study conclusions supported by the data and/or study design?' Use such examples to build the form's core prompts.
